title: Representativeness Heuristic
description: We judge the probability of something by how much it resembles a stereotype or a known category, ignoring base rates and logic.
shortDescription: We judge the probability of something by how much it resembles a stereotype or a known category, ignoring base rates and logic.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We judge the probability of something by how much it resembles a stereotype or a known category, ignoring base rates and logic.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A quiet, bookish person is assumed more likely to be a librarian than a salesperson, even though there are far more salespeople than librarians.
A startup founder who “looks like Steve Jobs” gets funded, despite a weaker business plan, because they fit the prototype.
A coin flip comes up T‑T‑T‑H‑T and people say it’s more random than T‑T‑T‑T‑T, even though all sequences are equally likely.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Judging people’s professions, trustworthiness, or intelligence by appearance.
Believing small sample results represent the whole (“The first three users loved it, so it’s a hit”).
Seeing patterns in randomness because they “look right.”

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “That seems about right.” (based on fit, not data)
“I got a read on them immediately.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re surprised when a stereotype doesn’t hold.
You assume that an anecdote or a small sample is representative.
You ignore base rates entirely because the “story” makes sense.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Categorization is efficient. The brain automatically matches new information to stored prototypes; this speeds up judgment but systematically misses statistical truths.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Explicitly ask: “What is the base rate?” before making probability judgments.
In personnel decisions, use structured interviews and blind evaluation where possible.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Believing that “you can tell” by looking.
Defending stereotypes because they “contain a grain of truth” without checking how large that grain actually is.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A hiring manager interviews a candidate who is articulate, well‑dressed, and confident. The candidate fits the mental image of a “top performer,” so the manager ignores lukewarm references. The candidate is hired and fails badly. The base rate of actual top performers is low, but the representativeness shortcut overrode it.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: “Looks the part” is the brain being lazy. The part is a set of behaviors, not a costume.
